extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in NLP / computational linguistics, media studies, and computational framing/narrative analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Using Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) and pretrained Transformer models to extract narrative elements (plot, characters, setting, moral) and compare framing/narratives between conspiracy and mainstream media across health-related topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: AMR suitability for narrative extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: AMR provides an expressive semantic representation of narrations and allows narrative elements (plot, characters, setting, moral of the story) to be directly mapped and extracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AMR parsing (with pretrained Transformer-based models) to extract narrative elements; the four elements of the narrative policy framework (Jones & McBeth, 2010) are directly applicable. Example claim: 'AMR is an ideal fit to analyze narrative frames, as we can directly extract context, characters, and plot from its graph representation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame selection using PropBank frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and analyze frames from PropBank (e.g., prevent-01, spread-03, vaccinate-01) to study narrative arguments and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage PropBank frame inventory (https://propbank.github.io/v3.4.0/frames/) and focus on relevant frames for the domain; compare frame usages across corpora (e.g., conspiracy vs mainstream).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ARG1 for frame interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: ARG1 is generally more suitable for the frames examined (it tended to have the highest scores), i.e., ARG1 often yields more meaningful narrative element assignments than ARG0 for the studied frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing frames such as prevent-01, spread-03, vaccinate-01, prioritize ARG1 distributions to identify over-representative narratives (authors observed ARG1 > ARG0 in suitability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative over-/under-representativeness scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute comparative scores to quantify over- and under-represented narrative elements between labels (e.g., conspiracy vs mainstream).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate by label and produce comparative occurrence/score tables (top-N highest and bottom-N lowest) to identify elements overrepresented for one label versus another; use these scores to highlight narrative differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding-space visualization with UMAP
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualize AMR-derived embedding space using UMAP dimensionality reduction so semantically similar words/element cluster together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UMAP was preferred over PCA/GloVe here because it better preserves semantic similarity; labels can be force-adjusted for readability and lines indicate moved labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model architecture: Transformer-based AMR parsing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pretrained Transformer models (e.g., BART with Penman decoder) for AMR parsing and downstream frame/narrative extraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors tried a BERT variant for topic modeling and SRL but found richer AMR representations via Transformer-based AMR parsing better suited. Example pipeline components: shared embedding lookup, BART model, Penman decoder, Frame Miner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: sentiment and indirect negation not encoded in AMR
rubrics_metrics.description: AMR does not directly encode subtle sentiment or indirect negations (only direct sentence polarity), limiting the extraction of e.g., hero/villain sentiment or prevent-like indirect negations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate external resources for sentiment analysis (e.g., polarity lexicons or models) and additional resources to detect indirect negation; naive sentiment-based subtype modeling is possible but outside AMR's native scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: perspective often not extractable
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspective is typically not part of the textual content and thus is not captured by AMR parsing in this setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that some narrative constructs (e.g., authorial perspective) may require other signals or metadata beyond sentence AMR graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings based on English datasets and the present approach may not generalize across other datasets, domains, languages, or more complex narratives without further research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform large-scale and rigorous experiments (including linguistic evaluation by experts) to validate explainability, effectiveness, reliability, and accuracy in new settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for expert linguistic evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative extraction and AMR-based mappings require human expert validation to assess linguistic quality and the constructs' validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement automatic analyses with expert annotations/linguistic evaluation to confirm that extracted narrative elements are meaningful and accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting dataset statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report detailed dataset statistics (e.g., number of documents, graphs, plots, unique characters/entities/settings/moral-of-the-story elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tables (e.g., Table 1) listing counts per document type and unique element counts to make the scale and coverage explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute handling in AMR embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes (e.g., names of entities) are arbitrary strings whose embeddings cannot be directly extracted from the AMR model; they do not possess a specific position in the embedding graph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit plotting attributes in embedding visualizations and instead refer to or provide the raw attribute data separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource and runtime considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: AMR parsing and the full pipeline require substantial compute: experiments were run on a SLURM-managed server with an Nvidia Quadro RTX 8000; each of the three subsets took approximately a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan compute resources and runtime expectations; times may vary with server utilization and hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative-theme indicators for conspiratorial vs mainstream media
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspiracy outlets emphasize belief/faith, urgency ('Today', 'Now') and immediacy ('You', 'I', 'We'), and one-sided war-framing; mainstream outlets focus more on institutions, scientific framing, and development/manufacturing topics in pharma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lexical and narrative element patterns (urgency tokens, pronoun usage, war/framing language, references to institutions vs people) as features to distinguish conspiratorial narratives from mainstream reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-reciprocity and corroborative emphasis as narrative signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspiracy media often include mainstream media as characters and frame themselves in opposition (corroborative emphasis on 'truth', 'true', 'actual'), while mainstream media do not reciprocally refer to conspiracists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mentions of 'mainstream' or media-as-character and recurrent truth-claims as indicators of conspiratorial framing; these patterns can be diagnostic in comparative analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-case caution: dual-use / downstream implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of conspiracy narratives can be used to improve detection and public guidance but could also enable better framing of conspiracy theories (dual-use risk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh and discuss societal impacts when publishing tools/data; consider mitigation measures (e.g., limiting release details that could be repurposed) and emphasize positive aims (countering misinformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of dimensionality-reduction and embedding source
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the model’s inherent embeddings (from the AMR/parser model) avoids domain shift and yields better mapping than using external pretrained embeddings (e.g., GloVe) in this study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer embeddings from the AMR/parsing model where possible for downstream semantic mapping; evaluate alternatives (PCA, pretrained embeddings) and select based on preservation of semantic similarity.
